# Wisdom of Solomon Chapter 7 — The EMET Bible (Literal)

**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** Codex Vaticanus, Wisdom 7 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/WIS_007_page_001.jpg

---

7:1 I myself also am mortal, the same as all others, and descended from the first-formed child of earth; and in the womb of a mother I was fashioned into flesh,

7:2 within the period of ten months, compacted in blood, from the seed of a man and the pleasure of sleep that goes with marriage.

7:3 And I too, when I was born, drew in the common air, and fell upon the earth that suffers all alike, and my first sound was a cry, as for all others.

7:4 I was nursed in swaddling clothes, and with care.

7:5 For no king has had any other beginning of existence;

7:6 there is for all one entrance into life, and a common departure.

7:7 Therefore I prayed, and understanding was given to me; I called upon God, and the spirit of wisdom came to me.

7:8 I preferred her to scepters and thrones, and I esteemed riches as nothing in comparison to her.

7:9 Neither did I liken to her any priceless gem, because all gold in her sight is a little sand, and silver will be counted as clay before her.

7:10 I loved her more than health and beauty, and I chose to have her rather than light, because her radiance never ceases.

7:11 But all good things came to me along with her, and in her hands uncountable riches.

7:12 And I rejoiced in them all, because wisdom leads them; though I did not know that she was their mother.

7:13 What I learned without guile I share without envy, and I do not pass by her wealth;

7:14 for she is an unfailing treasure for men, and those who get it win friendship with God, commended because of the gifts that come from her instruction.

7:15 May God grant me to speak with judgment, and to have thoughts worthy of what has been given to me; since he himself is the guide of wisdom and the corrector of the wise.

7:16 For both we and our words are in his hand, as well as all our understanding and skilled knowledge.

7:17 For he himself gave me unerring knowledge of what exists: to know the construction of the world and the activity of the elements;

7:18 the beginning and end and middle of times, the alterations of the solstices and the changes of the seasons,

7:19 the cycles of the year and the positions of the stars,

7:20 the natures of animals and the impulses of beasts, the power of the winds and the reasonings of men, the varieties of plants and the virtues of roots;

7:21 I learned both what is hidden and what is manifest, for wisdom, the fashioner of all things, taught me.

7:22 For in wisdom there is a spirit intelligent, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, mobile, clear, undefiled, distinct, invulnerable, loving the good, keen, unhindered, beneficent, philanthropic,

7:23 steadfast, sure, free from care, all-powerful, all-seeing, and penetrating through all spirits that are intelligent, pure, and altogether subtle.

7:24 For wisdom is more mobile than any motion; because of her purity she pervades and penetrates all things.

7:25 For she is a breath of the power of God, and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty; therefore nothing defiled gains entrance into her.

7:26 For she is a reflection of eternal light, a spotless mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness.

7:27 Although she is but one, she can do all things; and while remaining in herself, she renews all things; and age after age she enters into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets.

7:28 For God loves nothing so much as the man who lives with wisdom.

7:29 For she is more beautiful than the sun and excels every constellation of the stars; compared with light, she is found to be superior;

7:30 for night succeeds to light, but against wisdom evil does not prevail.

---

*EMET notes: The 21 attributes of Wisdom (vv. 22b–23) are: intelligent (noera), holy (hagia), unique (monogenes), manifold (polumerēs), subtle (leptotaton), mobile (eukinēton), clear (trancherēs), undefiled (amianton), distinct (saphes), invulnerable (aperanton), loving the good (philagathon), keen (oxu), unhindered (akōluton), beneficent (euergētikon), philanthropic (philanthrōpon), steadfast (bebaion), sure (asphaleis), free from care (amerimnon), all-powerful (pankrateis), all-seeing (panepiskopon), penetrating all things (dia pantōn chōroun). These 21 attributes influenced Christian pneumatology. Verse 25's "breath of the power of God" (atmis) and "emanation" (aporroia) are among the most philosophically precise descriptions of divine immanence in ancient literature.*
